items.title: The Best Affordable Ski Trips Across the U.S.
items.summary:
Skiers and boarders are gushing about El Niño again. The 2026-2027 winter won’t involve just any ENSO but a so-called Super El Niño. Potentially the biggest one on record, with exceptionally warm ocean temps on the West Coast hopefully sending a turbocharged jet stream across the U.S. According to my skiing friends, bartenders, and Trader Joe’s clerks, this could become the most memorable El Niño of our lives. Maybe .

While early signs do suggest that an epic season might be coming, we won’t know for sure until frequent storms continue to dump snow. It’s also uncertain where these potential storms may fall, though an El Niño typically sends winter weather toward the southern half of the country. Another question is whether a chance at great conditions warrants the risk of pricey reservations. And let’s be honest, we’ve all been burned before. Especially in recent years.

Climate change is shifting weather patterns, making snow forecasts more challenging. Rising global temps are causing more rain to fall at higher elevations. Meanwhile, skiing mega-corps have acquired most big-name resorts around the country, driving up lift tickets and inviting allegations of price-fixing . Plus, mountain town gentrification and nationwide inflation have skyrocketed the cost of lodging and meals out.

The estimated expense of an annual weeklong ski trip for a family of four now ranges from around $5,000 to over $15,000! That’s roughly the same budget as a small destination wedding, if you married a new person every single year. No surprise, last season’s poor Western conditions saw many…
items.t: The Best Affordable Ski Trips Across the U.S.

items.title: Endurance Athletes and the Myth of the Invincible Heart
items.summary:
Seth Ruhling was ten days away from racing in the 2023 World Mountain Running Championships when he first felt the pain. It woke him up. It tingled down his arm. It ached along the whole length of his spine. A nurse working out of the operating room at a local hospital in Louisville, Colorado, Ruhling took an aspirin just to be safe. Surely , he thought, this is not a heart thing. He got up and rolled out his back. He didn’t think much of it. He went to sleep.

The next morning, Ruhling pulled on his scrubs and went to work. The pain had not relented. He turned to one of the doctors on his floor and described the symptoms. The pain in his chest, the way it hurt when he bent over. At best, the doctor said, it’s nothing. At worst, he continued, you’re having an aortic dissection and you are about to die. Ruhling walked across the building and checked himself into his own hospital’s emergency room.

The answer was somewhere in between. Electrocardiograms (EKGs) and blood work told the story of a potential heart attack. Nurses and doctors who Ruhling knew personally turned, in that moment, from coworkers to aides. They hovered over him, checking in. It was then that Ruhling thought, maybe the worst is happening . He started mentally preparing himself. He realized he should call his wife in case he died. Thankfully, the worst was not happening. Despite the fact that so many of the signs pointed to a heart attack, those same signs also pointed to Ruhling’s official diagnosis: pericarditis—an inflammation of the pericardium, a sac of fibrous tissue that surrounds and protects the…
items.t: Endurance Athletes and the Myth of the Invincible Heart

items.title: The Winter Arc Challenge Is Trending. Here Are 3 Ways to Crush Your Fitness Goals When It’s Cold and Dark.
items.summary:
Many people press pause on their fitness goals this time of year as holiday plans take precedence, cold weather steamrolls gym motivation, and “I’ll get back on track in January” becomes a common refrain.

The Winter Arc Challenge urges the opposite. This viral social media trend, which first took off in 2024 and is buzzy again, encourages people to lock into their health and fitness goals for the last three months of the year, from October 1 to December 31. TikTok influencer Carly Berges came up with the term “Winter Arc,” according to an article published in Today .

“The Winter Arc is all about just dialing in and getting super laser-focused on your goals, on your personal development, on your growth so that way by the time of first of January rolls around, you are already coming out a whole ’nother beast,” Berges said in a TikTok video explaining the trend.

As a certified personal trainer and behavior change specialist, I’m a big proponent of sticking with fitness goals year-round, but I acknowledge this time of year can be especially tough for people—so I love the idea of a social media movement designed to help folks stay on track.

For anyone who wants to give it a whirl, I pulled together three of my favorite tips to boost gym motivation from now through December 31. Read on for the simple, effective hacks that can help you smash your winter fitness goals.

items.title: A Hiker Died Trying to Help His Son After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous
items.summary:
A hiker died on November 22 after reportedly slipping on ice and falling approximately 500 feet while trying to help his son on Mount Baden-Powell, a 9,399-foot peak in Southern California’s San Gabriel Mountains, according to a GoFundMe organized by the hiker’s niece.

The GoFundMe page identified the man as Guillermo Alejandro Batres. His niece, Jennifer Morse, wrote on the fundraising page that Batres and his son were attempting to summit the mountain when the younger man slipped and fell. When Batres tried to help him up, he lost his footing and fell down a steep gulch.

“On this mountain, there’s no room for error if you slip when it’s snowy or icy out,” Cris Hazzard, a Southern California hiking expert who has climbed Baden-Powell dozens of times, told Outside . “If you slip in the summer, you probably just fall on your butt, maybe go down some gravel. You slip in the winter, you’re going down hundreds, if not thousands, of feet.”

AV Scanner News , a local outlet that monitors emergency dispatches, reported that authorities received a call about the incident around 10:09 A.M. after the hikers encountered snow and ice roughly three miles from the Vincent Gap trailhead. Los Angeles County firefighters and sheriff’s deputies responded near mile marker 71 on Angeles Crest Highway. Authorities also requested the sheriff’s department’s Air Rescue 5 helicopter crew to recover Batres’s body, according to the outlet.

Authorities have not independently confirmed the family’s account of the fall, and the sheriff’s department did not respond to Outside ‘s request for comment…
items.t: A Hiker Died Trying to Help His Son After Winter Ice Turned a Popular Trail Dangerous

items.title: The Garmin CIRQA Is the Health Band for People Who Hate Wearing Watches
items.summary:
Overview: The Garmin CIRQA is an excellent screenless health band, but it suits people who dislike watches better than current Garmin watch wearers. After more than two months of day-and-night testing, Outside columnist Graham Averill found it tracks sleep, heart rate and HRV, auto-detects workouts and needs charging about once a week, all for $200 with no subscription. The trade-off: you can’t see your data in real time without opening your phone. 

I like wearing a big watch. Not a fancy watch, but a big, adventure watch with large numbers and all sorts of data on the face like the altitude of my current location and how many steps I’ve taken during the day. I like wearing a big adventure watch because it sends a statement to the world. It says, “I might be standing in the grocery store checkout line with a shocking amount of ground beef in my cart, but I do cool things in the outdoors.”

Also, my big adventure watch tracks all of my health data. I am a man of a certain age (50), so the world tells me constantly how important it is to monitor the hours I sleep and my resting heart rate. But Garmin recently released the CIRQA, a new health band that promises to track every aspect of my life, and it had me wondering if I should ditch the big, ostentatious watch and opt for a more minimalist health band. One without a face. One that sends a different statement to the world, probably along the lines of “please ask me about my meditation practices.”

So I spent the last two months wearing Garmin’s new CIRQA health band every day, and I discovered that it is an excellent…
